say.text: Worked example first. A 30-year-old fell from a scaffold: BP 90/60, pulse 118, pelvis unstable, GCS 14.
Read the plan through once. It has five steps, shown two screens at a time.

choices.label: I know this plan: test me now

say.text: 1. Two large-bore cannulas. If they fail, use intraosseous access.
2. Warmed isotonic crystalloid 1 L, then blood early. Warm everything given, to about 39 °C.
3. Pelvic binder over the greater trochanters.
Your classmate is managing a bleeder: 52-year-old, pelvic fracture, BP 84/50, pulse 120. Her plan has four steps and one wrong step.
1. Warmed isotonic crystalloid 1 L, then blood early. 2. Pelvic binder over the greater trochanters.
3. Tranexamic acid within 3 hours: 1 g over 10 minutes, then 1 g over 8 hours. 4. Urinary catheter first, to watch output. Which step is wrong?

choices.label: Step 1: warmed 1 L crystalloid, then blood early
Step 3: TXA within 3 h, then 1 g over 8 h
Step 4: urinary catheter first, to watch output
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Test each step against a rule you know. Ask which one puts a device in before a check that should come first.
That choice is not right.

Step 1 is correct. 2 L feels like the standard first bolus, but ATLS 10th edition gives 1 L warmed isotonic crystalloid in adults, then blood early. Exam note: older keys print 2 L; the current figure is 1 L.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the 2 litre figure is the belief to reset. The current adult bolus is 1 L.

say.text: That choice is not right.
Step 3 is correct as written. It looks wrong if you file 8 hours as the time limit. The 3 hours is the window for starting TXA after injury; the 8 hours is the length of the second infusion.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so re-anchor the TXA numbers: start window first, then infusion.

say.text: Yes. Step 4 puts a catheter in before the urethra is checked.
A catheter is contraindicated while urethral injury is suspected, until a urethrogram shows an intact urethra.
Another pelvic fracture, with blood at the urethral meatus. Why check the urethra before any catheter?

choices.label: A catheter is routine and drains urine, so it is safe first
Meatal blood means urethral injury until a urethrogram shows it intact
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what a catheter can do to a torn urethra, and which test shows whether the urethra is intact.
That choice is not right.
A catheter feels routine and harmless. But blood at the meatus means the urethra may be torn, and a blind catheter can worsen the tear, so the urethra is checked first.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the routine-catheter habit is the model to reset.

say.text: Yes. Meatal blood means the urethra may be torn, so the check comes before the catheter.
A retrograde urethrogram shows whether the urethra is intact; the catheter follows only if it is.
Next patient: an 8-year-old with facial burns. Intubation has failed and oxygen cannot be delivered. Which emergency surgical airway?

choices.label: Surgical cricothyroidotomy, the same as for an adult
Needle cricothyroidotomy, since the cricoid is at risk
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what the cricoid ring does in a child, and whether the adult rule still applies at this age.
That choice is not right.
The words surgical airway call up the adult rule. But under about 12 years surgical cricothyroidotomy is avoided, because the cricoid is at risk, so age changes the route.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the age qualifier before the airway rule.

say.text: Yes. Under about 12 years, surgical cricothyroidotomy risks damage to the cricoid, so a needle route is used.
Next: an adult with tension pneumothorax. Falling BP, one side silent, neck veins distended. Where do you decompress?

choices.label: 2nd intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line, the classic site
4th or 5th intercostal space, just anterior to mid-axillary line
Chest X-ray first, to confirm the side before decompressing
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which site the newest edition uses for adults, and what a short catheter does in a thick chest wall.
That choice is not right.

The 2nd space, mid-clavicular, is what older books and PYQ keys print, so it comes first to mind. In adults ATLS 10th edition moved the site to the 4th or 5th space, just anterior to the mid-axillary line.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the old site is the one to re-check against the edition.

say.text: That choice is not right.
A film feels like the careful step before a procedure. But tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis, and a patient in shock cannot wait for imaging.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so treat the X-ray as a reflex to drop, not a gate.

say.text: Yes. In an adult, decompress at the 4th or 5th intercostal space just anterior to the mid-axillary line.
The diagnosis is clinical, so decompression does not wait for an X-ray.
Two patients with the same tension pneumothorax: a 35-year-old and a 6-year-old. Which pair of sites is right?

choices.label: Both at the 2nd intercostal space, mid-clavicular, the classic site
Adult 4th or 5th ICS mid-axillary; child 2nd ICS mid-clavicular
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask whether one site can serve both patients, or whether age changes it.
That choice is not right.
Older texts give one classic site for everyone, so the age split looks like an extra rule. But ATLS 10th edition moved only the adult site: 4th or 5th space for adults, 2nd space for children.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the age split is the rule to learn.

say.text: Yes. ATLS 10th edition moved the adult site and kept the 2nd intercostal space for children.
Next: a 60-year-old after a fall. Flail chest on the left, oxygen saturation falling. What is the right management?

choices.label: Oxygen, analgesia, cautious fluids; ventilate if hypoxia persists
Urgent operative fixation of the flail segment, stopping the movement
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what is causing the low oxygen, not what is moving.
That choice is not right.
The moving segment is the visible sign, so treating it feels like treating the hypoxia. But the hypoxia comes from the pulmonary contusion beneath, so treatment goes to the lung.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the sign and the cause are different things.

say.text: Yes. The underlying pulmonary contusion causes the hypoxia, so treatment goes to the lung.
Next: pelvic fracture bleeding, and a head injury with GCS 7. What blood pressure target do you set?

choices.label: Accept a low pressure, to avoid popping the clot
Keep perfusion adequate for the brain, avoiding hypotension
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask whether a head injury changes the pressure target.
That choice is not right.
Permissive hypotension is a real rule for bleeding, so it feels right for any bleeder. But it is not used in traumatic brain injury, because a low pressure starves the injured brain.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check for a head injury before any low-pressure target.

say.text: Yes. Secondary brain injury follows low oxygen and low perfusion, so the brain needs adequate pressure.
Permissive hypotension is not used in traumatic brain injury.
Next: a bleeding trauma patient arrives 5 hours after injury. Is tranexamic acid still indicated?

choices.label: Yes, give it: TXA works for up to 8 hours after injury
No, the 3-hour window has passed, so withhold tranexamic acid
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask how long after injury TXA works, and what the 8 hours refers to.
That choice is not right.
The 8-hour figure sticks, so it gets filed as the time limit. But 8 hours is the length of the second infusion; the start window is 3 hours from injury, and at 5 hours it has passed.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the start window from the infusion duration.

say.text: Yes. Three hours is the window from injury; the 8 hours is the infusion once it has started.
Tranexamic acid is the antifibrinolytic of choice in bleeding trauma, within 3 hours.
Why does ATLS now give a smaller crystalloid bolus and bring blood in early?

choices.label: Large volumes dilute clotting factors and cool the patient
Two litres is the paediatric dose, too much for adults
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what large volumes of crystalloid do to clotting and to body temperature.
That choice is not right.
Two litres is the number older keys print, so it comes to mind. It was the adult figure in older editions and is not a paediatric dose. ATLS 10th edition gives 1 L warmed crystalloid and early blood.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the number itself is the thing to re-check.

say.text: Yes. Large crystalloid volumes dilute clotting factors and cool the patient, worsening bleeding.
So ATLS 10th edition gives 1 L warmed crystalloid in adults and brings blood early.
Next: a man with a chest wound answers your questions clearly at the door. When do the secondary survey and AMPLE history start?

choices.label: Right away, because a patient who talks is safe for now
After the primary survey, once resuscitation is under way
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what the primary survey must finish before the history begins.
That choice is not right.
A patient who talks feels safe, so the history seems ready to start. Talking shows a patent airway only for the moment; breathing and circulation are still unchecked, so the secondary survey waits.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so talking is reassurance, not a finished survey.

say.text: Yes. The secondary survey and AMPLE history follow the primary survey and resuscitation.
Next: pelvic fracture, no blood at the meatus yet, but the examiner finds a high-riding prostate. When is the catheter placed?

choices.label: Before anything else, to monitor urine output
After a urethrogram shows an intact urethra
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what a high-riding prostate says about the urethra.
That choice is not right.
Urine output is the usual reason for a catheter, so one seems right first. But a high-riding prostate means the urethra may be torn, so the urethrogram comes before any catheter.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so a high prostate is a reason to hold the catheter.

say.text: Yes. A high-riding prostate means the urethra may be torn, so the urethrogram comes first.
4. Tranexamic acid within 3 hours of injury: 1 g over 10 minutes, then 1 g over 8 hours.
5. Urethrogram first. The catheter follows only if the urethra is intact.
Large volumes of crystalloid dilute clotting factors and cool the patient, which worsens bleeding.
So the 10th edition starts with 1 L warmed isotonic crystalloid and brings blood in early. The 2 L key is the older exam answer.
TXA runs in two parts: 1 g over 10 minutes, then 1 g over 8 hours.
The clock that limits it is time from injury: start within 3 hours. The step in the plan keeps that order, so it is correct.
Blood at the meatus, perineal bruising or a high-riding prostate all suggest a urethral tear.
A retrograde urethrogram shows whether the urethra is intact. The catheter goes in only after an intact result.
In an adult, surgical cricothyroidotomy is the emergency surgical airway of choice.
In a child under about 12 years it is avoided and a needle route is used. Check the age before the airway rule.
ATLS 10th edition places the adult site at the 4th or 5th intercostal space, just anterior to the mid-axillary line.
The classic 2nd space is the older key and is kept for children. Exam note: use the edition the question names.
Tension pneumothorax is diagnosed at the bedside: shock, a silent side and distended neck veins.
Decompress at once. A film only delays the treatment that restores venous return.
Adults: 4th or 5th intercostal space, just anterior to the mid-axillary line.
Children: 2nd intercostal space, mid-clavicular line. The old key printed this one for all ages.
The paradoxical movement marks the injury. The contused lung underneath is what lowers the oxygen.
So the plan is oxygen, analgesia, cautious fluids, and ventilation if hypoxia persists.
Permissive hypotension accepts a lower pressure to avoid popping the clot, until bleeding is controlled.
With a head injury it is not used. Secondary brain injury follows low oxygen and low perfusion, so keep the pressure adequate.
TXA is given within 3 hours of injury: 1 g over 10 minutes, then 1 g over 8 hours.
The 3 hours limits when it may start. The 8 hours is only how long the second dose runs.
Large crystalloid volumes dilute clotting factors and cool the patient, which worsens bleeding.
So the 10th edition gives a smaller bolus, 1 L warmed in adults, and brings blood in early. Exam note: older keys print 2 L.
Talking shows a patent airway, for the moment. It does not clear the chest or the circulation.
The primary survey and resuscitation come first. The secondary survey and AMPLE history follow.
A high-riding prostate is a warning sign of urethral injury, as is blood at the meatus.
The retrograde urethrogram comes first. The catheter follows only if the urethra is intact.
